name: Productivity
tagline: Do the important work first and build habits that last.
description: Tools for prioritizing, protecting your focus and building routines, so your days move you toward your goals instead of only filling up.

messages.welcome: Being busy is easy. Being effective is a skill. Let's train it, one lesson at a time.
messages.comeback: No lecture about the gap. Start a 10-minute timer and do the next lesson. That is all.
messages.fail: You missed a few. Review the lesson calmly and try again, distraction-free this time.
messages.finished: You have the full toolkit: priorities, focus, habits, planning big projects and a system of your own. The real test is next Monday, so run your week with it.

lessons.title: Pick what matters with the Eisenhower box
lessons.content:
Imagine your schoolbag is too full to close. You have to take some things out. But which ones? The Eisenhower box helps you do the same with your tasks. You ask two questions about every task. Is it urgent, meaning it must happen soon? Is it important, meaning it really helps you or someone you care about? Two questions give you four boxes.

Without this, you just do whatever is loudest. A friend's message, a game notification, a small favour. At night you feel busy but nothing big got done. With the box, you spend your best time on what actually moves your life forward, and you stop feeling guilty about the stuff you skip.

Here's how the four boxes work. Box 1 is urgent and important, like homework due tomorrow. Do it now. Box 2 is important but not urgent, like practising English every day or revising for an exam that is a month away. Put it on your calendar with a time. Box 3 is urgent but not important, like a friend asking you to check their Facebook post right now. Keep it short or hand it to someone else. Box 4 is neither, like watching random videos. Drop it.

To try it, write 8 to 10 tasks on paper. Draw a big plus sign to make four boxes. Put each task in one box. Then do Box 1 first, give Box 2 a fixed time, make Box 3 quick, and cross out Box 4. Box 2 is the secret. Those tasks never shout at you, so they get pushed aside forever unless you give them a time.

Take Rafi, class 8. Every evening he answered group chats, helped his cousin with a game and watched cricket clips. His maths test was in three weeks, so it never felt urgent. He drew the box. Maths revision went into Box 2, so he gave it 30 minutes every day at 7 pm. Cricket clips went into Box 4. Three weeks later he walked into the test calm instead of cramming the night before.

The common mistake is thinking urgent means important. A ringing phone feels important because it is loud, but most of the time it is Box 3. Before you jump on something, ask: if I do this an hour later, will anything bad happen? If not, it is not Box 1.

Remember: do Box 1, schedule Box 2, shrink Box 3, drop Box 4.
key_points: Ask two questions about each task: is it urgent, and is it important?
Do urgent and important tasks now, and give important but not urgent tasks a fixed time.
Keep urgent but unimportant tasks short, and drop tasks that are neither.
Loud does not mean important, so check before you jump.
lessons.tip: Pick one Box 2 task tonight and write the exact time you will do it tomorrow, like "English practice, 5:00 pm".
lessons.task: Write 8 things on your mind, draw the four boxes, and put each thing in a box. Circle one Box 2 task and give it a time this week.

quiz.q: Rafi's maths test is three weeks away. Which box does revising for it go in?
options: Important but not urgent, so he schedules it
Urgent and important, so he does it all tonight
Urgent but not important, so he keeps it short
Neither, so he drops it
quiz.explain: The test matters but is not due yet. That is Box 2, so you give it a fixed time.

quiz.q: What should you do with a task that is urgent but not important?
options: Drop it completely without thinking
Keep it short or hand it to someone else
Put it on your calendar for next month
Do it before everything else
quiz.explain: Box 3 tasks need a quick reply or someone else, not your best time.

quiz.q: Which question helps you check if a task is really Box 1?
options: Is this task the loudest one right now?
Will this task take less than five minutes?
If I do this an hour later, will anything bad happen?
Did a friend ask me to do this?
quiz.explain: If nothing bad happens when you wait, the task only feels urgent. It is not Box 1.

lessons.title: Focus blocks and the Pomodoro timer
lessons.content:
Think of your focus like a phone battery. It runs down as you use it, and it needs short charging breaks. The Pomodoro method uses this idea. You work on one thing for 25 minutes with a timer, then rest for 5 minutes. One 25-minute round is called a pomodoro, which is Italian for tomato, because the man who invented it used a tomato-shaped kitchen timer.

Without a timer, studying turns into "sitting with the book open". You read a line, check your phone, read another line, get a snack. Two hours pass and you did maybe 30 real minutes. With a timer, starting is easier because 25 minutes feels small, and the break stops your brain from getting tired and bored.

Here's how to do one round. First, pick exactly one task, like "solve 10 maths problems", not "study". Second, put your phone in another room or face down on silent. Third, set a timer for 25 minutes and work only on that task. If a thought pops up, like "I need to text Nusrat", write it on a scrap paper and go back to work. Fourth, when the timer rings, stop and take 5 minutes to stand, drink water or stretch. No phone scrolling in the break, because 5 minutes of scrolling easily becomes 20.

After four rounds, take a longer break of 15 to 30 minutes. So two hours of study looks like four rounds of 25 minutes with short breaks in between. If 25 minutes feels too long at first, start with 15 and add 5 minutes each week. The number is not magic. The rule is: one task, no distractions, then a real rest.

Nusrat, class 9, had to learn a long biology chapter. She kept opening Facebook every few minutes and finished only two pages in an evening. She tried pomodoros. Round one: read pages 1 to 3. Round two: pages 4 to 6. In the breaks she drank water and looked out of the window. After four rounds she had finished the chapter and still had time to watch a drama with her mother.

The common mistake is skipping the break because you feel you are "on a roll". It feels good for a while, but your focus drops later and you burn out by round three. Take the break even when you don't want to.

Remember: one task, 25 minutes, phone away, then 5 minutes of real rest.
key_points: A pomodoro is 25 minutes of work on one task, then a 5-minute break.
After four rounds, take a longer 15 to 30 minute break.
Write down distracting thoughts on paper instead of acting on them.
Breaks should rest your brain, so skip phone scrolling during them.
lessons.tip: Keep a small scrap paper next to you during a pomodoro and write every "I should also..." thought on it, then deal with them after the round.
lessons.task: Pick one small study task, put your phone in another room, and do one 25-minute pomodoro right now, followed by a 5-minute break without your phone.

quiz.q: How long is one normal pomodoro work round?
options: 25 minutes
5 minutes
45 minutes
60 minutes
quiz.explain: The classic round is 25 minutes of focused work followed by a 5-minute break.

quiz.q: During a round, you suddenly remember you need to text Nusrat. What should you do?
options: Text her quickly, it only takes a minute
Stop the timer and start over later
Write it on scrap paper and get back to work
Keep thinking about it until the round ends
quiz.explain: Writing it down clears your mind without breaking your focus.

quiz.q: Why is scrolling a bad idea during the 5-minute break?
options: Scrolling uses up your phone's battery
Five minutes of scrolling easily turns into 20 and doesn't rest your brain
You are not allowed to touch the phone all day
The break should be used for more studying
quiz.explain: The break is for real rest, like water and stretching. Scrolling steals time and attention.

lessons.title: Find out where your time goes
lessons.content:
Say your pocket money keeps disappearing and you don't know how. The easy fix is to write down every taka you spend for a few days. Time works the same way. A time log means writing down what you actually did, every hour or so, for a few days. Then you can see where your hours really go, not where you think they go.

Most people guess wrong. You might think you study 3 hours a day, but your log shows 1 hour of study and 2 hours of "quick checks" on your phone. Without a log, you try to fix the wrong thing. With a log, you find the real leak, and even saving one hour a day gives you 7 extra hours a week.

Here's how to do it. Take a small notebook or the notes app. Every hour, or whenever you switch activities, write the time and what you did, like "4:00 to 4:40, tuition homework" or "4:40 to 5:30, YouTube". Be honest. Nobody else will see it. Do this for 3 days, including one holiday, because weekends often look very different.

At the end, add up the time in a few groups: study, sleep, eating, travel, phone or TV, family, play. Look for two things. First, the biggest surprise, the group that is much bigger than you expected. Second, small gaps, like 20 minutes waiting for the school bus, that you could use for revision cards. Pick just one change to make, not ten.

Sabbir, class 10, felt he never had time for his SSC prep. He logged three days. The result shocked him: about 2.5 hours a day on his phone, mostly in small 10-minute chunks after every meal. He also spent 40 minutes daily stuck in traffic going to coaching. His change: no phone at the dinner table, and vocabulary cards in the car. In a week he found nearly an hour a day without giving up anything he loved.

The common mistake is filling the log at night from memory. You will forget the small chunks, and the small chunks are exactly where time hides. Write it during the day, right when you switch.

Remember: you can't fix your time until you see it, so log it honestly for three days.
key_points: A time log is a simple record of what you actually did through the day.
Log for 3 days, including a holiday, and write it as you go, not at night.
Add the time into groups and look for the biggest surprise.
Make one change based on what you find, not ten.
lessons.tip: Set a quiet alarm every hour for the three days. When it buzzes, write one line in your log and get back to what you were doing.
lessons.task: Start your time log now: write what you did in each hour since you woke up today, as honestly as you can, and keep it going until bedtime.

quiz.q: Why should you write the time log during the day instead of at night?
options: Writing at night keeps you awake too long
The log only counts if it is written in the morning
You forget the small chunks, and that's where time hides
Nobody can check a log written at night
quiz.explain: Memory skips the 10-minute bits, but those add up to hours.

quiz.q: What did Sabbir find when he logged his time?
options: About 2.5 hours a day on his phone in small chunks
He was studying too much and needed rest
He was sleeping 12 hours a day
His coaching classes were too long
quiz.explain: His log showed small phone checks after meals adding up to a lot.

quiz.q: After adding up your log, what should you do next?
options: Pick one change to make based on the biggest surprise
Change ten habits at once to fix everything
Throw the log away, it has done its job
Log for another month before changing anything
quiz.explain: One focused change is easier to keep than many at once.

lessons.title: A to-do list that actually works
lessons.content:
A to-do list is like a shopping list for your day. You write what you need to get done so your brain doesn't have to remember it all. But a messy list is like a shopping list that says "food". You reach the bazar and still don't know what to buy. A good to-do list is short, clear, and tells you exactly what to do next.

Without a good list, you either forget things, like the science project due Thursday, or you write 25 tasks, finish 4, and feel like a failure. A good list makes starting easy, because every item is a clear action, and it makes you feel good at night because you actually finished what you planned.

Here are the rules. Rule one: start each task with a verb and make it small. Not "science project" but "find 3 pictures of the water cycle". If a task takes more than an hour, break it into smaller pieces. Rule two: keep today's list to 3 to 5 items. Put everything else on a separate "later" list so it doesn't crowd your day.

Rule three: star your top 1 task, the one that matters most if you only finish one thing. Do it first, before the easy stuff. Rule four: write tomorrow's list the night before, in 5 minutes. When you wake up, you already know where to start, so you don't waste the morning deciding. At night, move unfinished tasks to tomorrow or the later list, and cross out anything that no longer matters.

Tania, class 7, wrote lists like "Bangla, English, project, tuition, clean room, call Nanu". Every day half of it stayed undone. She rewrote it: star task "write the first paragraph of the Bangla essay", then "do English exercise 4", "call Nanu after Maghrib". Only three items, each one clear. She finished them by evening and the rest waited on her later list without bothering her.

The common mistake is writing vague, giant tasks like "study for exams". Your brain doesn't know where to begin, so it picks something easier, like your phone. If you look at a task and don't know the first step, rewrite it until you do.

Remember: short list, clear verbs, star one task, and do the star first.
key_points: Start every task with a verb and make it small enough to finish in under an hour.
Keep today's list to 3 to 5 items and park the rest on a later list.
Star your most important task and do it first.
Write tomorrow's list the night before so the morning starts fast.
lessons.tip: If a task has sat on your list for three days, ask "what is the very first 10-minute step?" and replace the task with that step.
lessons.task: Write tomorrow's to-do list now: 3 to 5 items, each starting with a verb, with one starred task you will do first.

quiz.q: Which of these is the best to-do list item?
options: Science project
Study
Work on school stuff
Find 3 pictures of the water cycle
quiz.explain: It starts with a verb and is small and clear, so you know exactly what to do.

quiz.q: How many items should today's list usually have?
options: 3 to 5
1 at most
As many as you can think of
quiz.explain: A short list is doable and keeps you from feeling like you failed.

quiz.q: What did Tania change to finish her list?
options: She added more tasks to stay busy
She stopped writing lists altogether
She did the easy tasks first to warm up
She made each item small and clear and kept only three
quiz.explain: Clear, small items and a short list made her day finishable.

lessons.title: Habits that stick
lessons.content:
A habit is something you do almost without thinking, like brushing your teeth after waking up. You don't sit and decide every morning. Your brain just does it. Imagine if reading 10 pages or doing 5 maths problems worked the same way. That's what building a habit means: turning a good action into something automatic.

Without habits, every good thing needs willpower, and willpower runs out by evening. That's why "I'll study daily from tomorrow" usually lasts three days. With a habit, the action happens on autopilot, and small actions repeated daily add up. Ten new English words a day is over 3,600 words in a year.

Here's the trick: tie the new habit to something you already do every day. Use this sentence: "After I [old habit], I will [new habit]." For example, "After I eat lunch, I will read 2 pages" or "After Fajr, I will do 10 push-ups." The old habit acts like an alarm that reminds you.

Next, make the habit tiny at first, so small that you can't say no. Not "study 2 hours" but "open the maths book and do 1 problem". Once you start, you often do more, but even 1 problem counts. Make it easy to start by keeping the book on your table, already open. Then track it: put a tick on a calendar each day. Seeing a row of ticks makes you not want to break the chain.

Rafi wanted to read more storybooks, but he kept forgetting. He wrote: "After I finish dinner, I will read 2 pages." He kept the book on his pillow so he would see it. Some nights he read 2 pages, some nights 20. He put a tick on the wall calendar each night. After a month he had 28 ticks and had finished three books, more than he read in the whole previous year.

The common mistake is starting too big. People decide to wake at 5, run, study 3 hours and quit sugar, all on the same day. By day four everything collapses. Start with one tiny habit, keep it for two or three weeks, then add the next one. And if you miss a day, never miss two in a row.

Remember: after an old habit, do a tiny new one, make it easy, and tick it every day.
key_points: Link a new habit to an old one: "After I ___, I will ___."
Start so small you can't say no, like 1 problem or 2 pages.
Make it easy to start and tick a calendar each day you do it.
If you miss a day, never miss two in a row.
lessons.tip: Put the thing you need for your habit where you'll trip over it: the book on your pillow, the skipping rope by the door.
lessons.task: Write one sentence: "After I ___, I will ___" with a habit that takes under 2 minutes, then set up the thing you need for it right now.

quiz.q: Which habit sentence follows the method in this lesson?
options: After I eat lunch, I will read 2 pages
I will read more books this year
I will study whenever I feel motivated
I will read 50 pages every single day
quiz.explain: It links the new habit to an old one and keeps it tiny.

quiz.q: Why should a new habit start tiny?
options: Because big habits are not allowed
So it's too easy to say no to, and you keep doing it
Because small habits don't count for anything
So you can finish it in one day and stop
quiz.explain: A tiny habit doesn't need willpower, so it survives on tired days.

quiz.q: Rafi missed one night of reading. What does the lesson say to do?
options: Start the whole habit again from zero
Read 40 pages next night to make up for it
Give up, the chain is broken
Read the next night and never miss two in a row
quiz.explain: One miss is normal. Two in a row is how habits die.

lessons.title: The weekly review
lessons.content:
A cricket team doesn't just play match after match. After each game, the coach sits with the players and asks: what went well, what went wrong, what do we change next time? A weekly review is that coach meeting, but for your own week. Once a week, you spend 15 to 20 minutes looking back at the last seven days and planning the next seven.

Without it, weeks just happen to you. The same problems repeat, like always running late on Monday or forgetting tuition homework, and you never notice the pattern. Tasks you wrote down get lost. With a review, you catch problems early, you start each week knowing your top goals, and you feel in control instead of chasing things.

Here's how to run it. Pick a fixed time, like Friday after Jumma or Saturday evening. Step one, look back: open your to-do list, calendar and notes. Tick what got done. Ask three questions and write short answers: What went well? What went badly? What will I do differently? Step two, clear up: move unfinished tasks to next week or delete them, and empty any notes or papers you collected into your list.

Step three, look ahead: check next week's calendar for tests, deadlines, birthdays and family events. Then choose your top 3 goals for the week, like "finish chemistry chapter 4", "submit art project", "practise bowling three times". Write them at the top of your list. During the week, whenever you're unsure what to do next, look at those three.

Nusrat kept getting surprised by class tests. Every Saturday evening she started a 15-minute review with a cup of tea. On the first Saturday she noticed she'd forgotten two homework tasks because they were written on random pages. She moved everything into one list. When she looked ahead, she spotted a physics test on Wednesday and planned 30 minutes for it on Monday and Tuesday. No more panic on Tuesday nights.

The common mistake is turning the review into a guilt session, where you only list what you failed at and feel bad. That makes you skip it next week. Spend equal time on what went well, keep it short, and focus on one thing to change.

Remember: once a week, look back, clear up, and pick your top 3 for next week.
key_points: A weekly review is 15 to 20 minutes to look back and plan ahead.
Ask: what went well, what went badly, what will I change?
Move or delete unfinished tasks and check next week's calendar.
Choose your top 3 goals for the coming week.
lessons.tip: Tie your review to something you already do weekly, like after Jumma prayer or after Friday family lunch, so you don't forget it.
lessons.task: Do a mini review now: write what went well this week, one thing that went badly, and your top 3 goals for next week.

quiz.q: What are the three steps of the weekly review in this lesson?
options: Wake up, study, sleep
Plan, panic, catch up
Write, delete, forget
Look back, clear up, look ahead
quiz.explain: You review the past week, tidy loose tasks, then plan the next week.

quiz.q: How did Nusrat stop getting surprised by tests?
options: She studied every subject every night
She checked next week's calendar during her review and planned time early
She asked her friends the night before each test
She stopped writing anything down
quiz.explain: Looking ahead showed her the Wednesday test early enough to plan.

quiz.q: What is the common mistake people make with weekly reviews?
options: Spending too long on what went well
Doing it on the same day every week
Choosing only three goals
Only listing failures, which makes them want to skip it
quiz.explain: A guilt session feels bad, so people stop doing it. Balance it.

lessons.title: Turn repeated work into templates
lessons.content:
Think about how your mother makes rice. She doesn't invent a new method every day. She knows the steps: wash, add water, boil, lower the heat. A template is the same idea for your own repeated work. It's a ready-made pattern or checklist you reuse, so you don't start from zero every time.

Without templates, you waste time and energy redoing the same thinking. Every time you pack for school, you try to remember everything and forget your geometry box. Every essay starts with a blank page and ten minutes of staring. With templates, repeated jobs get faster, you make fewer mistakes, and your brain is free for the parts that actually need thinking.

Here's how to make one. First, notice what you do again and again, like packing your school bag, writing an essay, preparing for a test, or sending a message to your tuition teacher. Second, the next time you do it, write the steps down as you go. Third, save that list somewhere easy, like a page in your notebook or a note on your phone, and give it a clear name, like "School bag checklist".

A few examples. School bag checklist: timetable books, homework copies, geometry box, water bottle, tiffin, ID card. Essay template: opening line that answers the question, three paragraphs each with one point and one example, a short ending. Test prep template: list chapters, mark weak topics, solve 10 past questions, review mistakes. Each time you use a template, fix anything that was missing.

Sabbir forgot something almost every morning, his ID card one day, his calculator the next. His teacher made him stand outside class twice. He wrote a six-item checklist on a card and stuck it near the door. Every night he packed while reading the card. In a month he didn't forget a single thing, and packing took 3 minutes instead of a frantic 10 in the morning.

The common mistake is making templates too long and fancy, with 30 steps for packing a bag. Nobody uses those. Keep a template to the steps you actually forget or repeat, usually 5 to 8 lines, and keep it where you'll see it while doing the job.

Remember: if you do something more than twice, write the steps once and reuse them.
key_points: A template is a ready-made checklist or pattern for work you repeat.
Write the steps the next time you do the job, then save and name it.
Keep templates short, 5 to 8 lines, and put them where you'll see them.
Improve the template each time you notice something missing.
lessons.tip: Stick your checklist exactly where the job happens: the bag list by the door, the study list inside your desk drawer.
lessons.task: Pick one thing you do every day or week, like packing your bag, and write a 5 to 8 line checklist for it right now.

quiz.q: What is a template in this lesson?
options: A new plan you make from scratch each time
A list of everything you must do in your life
A ready-made checklist or pattern you reuse for repeated work
A timer that tells you when to stop working
quiz.explain: It saves you from re-thinking the same steps every time.

quiz.q: How did Sabbir stop forgetting things for school?
options: He packed his bag in the morning in a hurry
He asked his mother to pack for him
He carried every book every day
He used a six-item checklist near the door each night
quiz.explain: A short checklist in the right place fixed the problem.

quiz.q: Why should a template stay short, around 5 to 8 lines?
options: Short templates look nicer
Teachers only allow short lists
Long fancy templates don't get used
Long templates are hard to print
quiz.explain: Keep only the steps you forget or repeat, so it's quick to follow.

lessons.title: Capture everything in one trusted inbox
lessons.content:
Imagine you had five piggy banks hidden around the house and you put coins in whichever was closest. You'd never know how much you have, and some coins would be lost forever. That's what happens when your tasks and ideas are scattered across your head, sticky notes, WhatsApp chats and the back of your copy. An inbox is one single place where every task, idea and reminder goes first.

Without one inbox, things slip. Your teacher says "bring a chart paper on Sunday", you think you'll remember, and on Sunday you don't. Your brain also stays busy trying to hold everything, which makes you anxious and tired. With one trusted inbox, you write it down and let it go, because you know you'll see it later.

Here's how to set it up. Choose one place you always have with you: a small notebook in your bag, or one note on your phone called "Inbox". The rule is simple: the moment something comes up, a task, a date, an idea, write it there in a few words. "Chart paper Sunday." "Ask Abbu about bKash for exam fee." Don't organize it yet. Just catch it.

The second half matters just as much: empty the inbox once a day, for example in the evening for 5 minutes. Go through each line and decide. If it takes under 2 minutes, do it now. If it has a date, put it on your calendar. If it's a task, move it to your to-do list. If it's just an idea, move it to an ideas page or delete it. Then cross it out of the inbox.

Tania kept missing small things: a friend's birthday, a form her mother had to sign, a book to return to the library. They were all in her head or in random chats. She made a phone note called Inbox and wrote everything in it the moment she heard it. Each night after dinner she cleared it in 5 minutes. That month she didn't miss a single form, and she said her head felt lighter.

The common mistake is having two or three inboxes, like one notebook, one phone note and some sticky notes. Then you're back to hidden piggy banks. Pick one, and if something lands somewhere else, copy it into your one inbox that day.

Remember: catch everything in one place right away, and empty it every day.
key_points: An inbox is one single place where every task, date and idea goes first.
Write things down the moment they come up, in a few words.
Empty the inbox once a day: do it, schedule it, move it or delete it.
Use only one inbox, not several.
lessons.tip: If a task takes less than 2 minutes, like replying "yes" to your tuition teacher, do it right when you clear your inbox instead of writing it anywhere else.
lessons.task: Create your one inbox now, a notebook page or a phone note named "Inbox", and write down every task or idea currently in your head.

quiz.q: What should you do the moment a new task comes up?
options: Try hard to remember it
Organize it into your calendar right away
Tell a friend so they can remind you
Write it in your one inbox in a few words
quiz.explain: Catching it fast means you don't have to hold it in your head.

quiz.q: While clearing the inbox, a task takes about one minute. What do you do?
options: Do it right now
Move it to next week's list
Delete it because it's too small
Copy it into a second inbox
quiz.explain: Under-2-minute tasks are faster to do than to file.

quiz.q: What is the common mistake with inboxes?
options: Emptying it every day
Writing tasks in only a few words
Having two or three inboxes in different places
Keeping it on your phone
quiz.explain: Several inboxes bring back the problem of scattered tasks.

lessons.title: Beat procrastination
lessons.content:
Procrastination means putting off something you know you should do, and doing something easier instead. It's like standing at the edge of a cold pond. The water isn't that bad once you're in, but the first step feels awful, so you keep standing there. Most of the time, we don't avoid the task. We avoid the bad feeling at the start of it.

Putting things off feels nice for an hour, but it costs a lot later. The work doesn't go away, it just gets squeezed into the last night, so you sleep late, make silly mistakes and feel guilty the whole time you're "relaxing". When you learn to start early, the same work takes less time and you actually enjoy your free time.

Here are three tricks to get into the water. Trick one: the 5-minute rule. Tell yourself, "I'll do just 5 minutes, then I can stop." Starting is the hardest part, and after 5 minutes most people keep going. Trick two: make the first step tiny and exact. Not "write the essay" but "write the title and the first sentence". A small step feels less scary.

Trick three: remove the easy escape. If your phone is the place you run to, put it in another room before you start. Also notice your excuses. "I'll do it when I feel ready" is a trap, because the feeling of being ready usually comes after you start, not before. And when you finish a hard task, give yourself a small reward, like a cup of tea or one episode of your favourite show.

Sabbir had a history assignment due Thursday. On Monday and Tuesday he kept saying "later" and played games instead. On Wednesday he tried the 5-minute rule: phone in the drawing room, timer set, first step "write three facts about the Language Movement". After 5 minutes he didn't want to stop. He finished in 70 minutes, slept on time, and submitted it calmly. Next time he started on day one.

The common mistake is thinking procrastination means you are lazy. It usually means the task feels confusing or too big. Instead of blaming yourself, ask: "What's the very next small step?" Shrinking the task works far better than scolding yourself.

Remember: you don't need to feel ready, just start for 5 minutes with a tiny first step.
key_points: Procrastination is mostly avoiding the bad feeling at the start of a task.
Use the 5-minute rule: start for just 5 minutes, then decide.
Make the first step tiny and exact, and remove easy escapes like the phone.
Feeling ready comes after you start, not before.
lessons.tip: When you catch yourself saying "later", say out loud the next tiny step, like "open the copy and write the date", and do only that.
lessons.task: Pick one task you've been putting off, write its tiny first step, put your phone away, and work on it for just 5 minutes now.

quiz.q: What is the 5-minute rule?
options: Take a 5-minute break after every page
Finish any task within 5 minutes
Tell yourself you'll work only 5 minutes, then you can stop
Wait 5 minutes before starting anything
quiz.explain: Starting is the hardest part, and 5 minutes makes it feel easy.

quiz.q: What was Sabbir's tiny first step?
options: Finish the whole assignment in one go
Watch a documentary first
Write three facts about the Language Movement
Clean his whole room before starting
quiz.explain: A small, exact first step made it easy to begin.

quiz.q: According to the lesson, procrastination usually means what?
options: The task feels confusing or too big
You are a lazy person
You don't care about school
You need more sleep every night
quiz.explain: Shrinking the task works better than blaming yourself.

lessons.title: Tame digital distractions
lessons.content:
Your phone is like a friend who taps your shoulder every two minutes saying "look at this!" Each tap seems small. But every time you look, your brain has to climb back into the work, and that takes time. Digital distractions are all the pings, notifications and "just a quick check" moments from your phone, computer and TV that pull your attention away.

Here's why it matters. After an interruption, it can take several minutes to get your full focus back. If your phone buzzes 20 times in an evening, you never reach deep focus at all. Your study becomes slow and shallow, you remember less, and the work stretches late into the night. With distractions under control, one hour of real focus can beat three hours of interrupted work.

The trick is to make distractions harder to reach, instead of relying on willpower. Step one: turn off notifications for every app that isn't about people who really need you, like games, shopping and social media. Keep calls from family on. Step two: while studying, put your phone in another room, or at least face down and out of reach. Out of sight really helps.

Step three: give your phone a fixed time. For example, check messages only in your breaks, or for 15 minutes after each hour of study. Step four: move tempting apps off your home screen into a folder, so opening them takes an extra moment of thought. If you study on a computer, close every tab except the one you need. Small hurdles stop the automatic reach.

Nusrat studied with her phone next to her book. Messenger, Facebook and a game all sent alerts. She'd sit for 2 hours and finish one exercise. She turned off all notifications except calls, kept the phone in her mother's room while studying, and allowed herself 10 minutes of phone time after each pomodoro set. The same homework now took 50 minutes, and she had her evening free.

The common mistake is keeping the phone on the desk "just in case" and promising not to look. Even a silent phone in view pulls at your attention, because part of your brain keeps wondering what's on it. Distance beats promises.

Remember: notifications off, phone out of sight, and check it only at set times.
key_points: Every interruption costs you minutes of getting your focus back.
Turn off notifications for apps that don't really need you.
Keep your phone out of sight while studying, not just silent.
Give phone checking fixed times, like during breaks.
lessons.tip: Open your phone settings today and switch off notifications for every game and social app. It takes 5 minutes and saves hours.
lessons.task: Go through your phone right now and turn off notifications for at least 3 apps, then move your most tempting app off the home screen.

quiz.q: Why is a phone that buzzes 20 times an evening a problem even if you only look for a second?
options: The phone battery runs out faster
After each interruption it takes minutes to get your full focus back
Your parents will be angry
It makes the phone slower
quiz.explain: The real cost is climbing back into focus, not the second you looked.

quiz.q: Which change did Nusrat NOT make?
options: She turned off all notifications except calls
She kept the phone on her desk and promised not to look
She kept the phone in her mother's room while studying
She allowed 10 minutes of phone time after each set
quiz.explain: She used distance, not promises. A phone in view still pulls your attention.

quiz.q: What is better than promising yourself not to look at your phone?
options: Turning the brightness down
Putting the phone out of sight, in another room
Keeping it face up so you see it's quiet
Holding it in your hand while you read
quiz.explain: Distance beats promises because out of sight really is out of mind.

lessons.title: Say no to protect your yes
lessons.content:
Your time is like a plate at a wedding buffet. It can only hold so much. If you say yes to every dish someone offers, there's no room left for the biryani you actually came for. Saying no politely is how you keep space on your plate for the things that matter most to you.

Without saying no, your day fills up with other people's plans. You agree to join every game, help with every favour, go to every hangout, and then your own homework, practice or rest gets squeezed into late night. You end up tired, behind and a bit annoyed with everyone. When you can say a kind no, your yes means more, and you have time for your own goals.

Here's how to do it. First, know your yes: what are your 1 to 3 priorities this week, like exams, cricket practice or helping at home? Anything that clashes with those needs a careful look. Second, don't answer instantly. Say, "Let me check and tell you in an hour." This pause stops you from saying yes just because it's awkward to refuse.

Third, say no kindly and clearly, with a short reason if you like, and no long excuses. "Thanks for asking! I can't come today, I have a test tomorrow." Fourth, offer a smaller yes or another time if you genuinely want to help: "I can't play this evening, but I'm free Friday afternoon." With adults like parents and teachers, don't just refuse. Explain your plan politely and ask, for example, "Can I do this after my test on Thursday?"

Tania was the person everyone asked for help. In one week she agreed to design a friend's poster, join two group chats' events and help her cousin with homework. Her own science project was left until the night before. Next week she tried: "I'd love to help, but I can't this week. Next Saturday I can." Her friends were fine with it. She finished her project on time and still helped her cousin on Saturday.

The common mistake is giving a long, guilty explanation. The longer your excuse, the more it sounds like you can be talked into it. A short, warm no is kinder and clearer for everyone.

Remember: know your priorities, pause before you answer, and say a short, kind no.
key_points: Saying no to some things keeps time for what matters most to you.
Know your 1 to 3 priorities, and pause before answering a request.
Say no kindly and clearly, with a short reason, not long excuses.
Offer a smaller yes or another time when you want to help.
lessons.tip: Practise one line you can use anywhere: "Thanks for asking! I can't this time, but I hope it goes great." Say it out loud a few times so it comes easily.
lessons.task: Write your top 3 priorities for this week, then write one polite no sentence and one "smaller yes" sentence you could use for a request you often get.

quiz.q: Someone asks you to join something. What does the lesson suggest before answering?
options: Say yes right away so they're not upset
Ignore the message completely
Pause and say you'll check and reply soon
Say no to everything without thinking
quiz.explain: A short pause stops you from saying yes only because refusing feels awkward.

quiz.q: Which reply is the best kind of no?
options: Sorry sorry sorry, it's just that my mother might maybe need me and also I have so much...
Thanks for asking! I can't come today, I have a test tomorrow.
No.
Maybe, I'll see, ask me again later.
quiz.explain: It is short, warm and clear, with one simple reason.

quiz.q: What did Tania offer instead of a full yes?
options: Money instead of time
Help next Saturday instead of this week
To do everyone's work at night
To quit her science project
quiz.explain: A smaller yes or a different time lets you help without losing your own priorities.

lessons.title: One thing at a time, small tasks in a batch
lessons.content:
Try patting your head and rubbing your tummy while reciting a poem. You'll mess up at least one. Your brain can't truly do two thinking tasks at once. When you "multitask", it actually switches back and forth very fast, and each switch costs a little time and attention. Single-tasking means doing one thing until it's done or until a planned stop. Batching means grouping small similar tasks and doing them together in one go.

Switching makes you slower and sloppier. If you write an essay while replying to chats, the essay takes longer and has more mistakes, and the replies are half-hearted too. Small tasks scattered through the day, like replying to messages or tidying your desk, each break your focus. Single-tasking gives you deeper, faster work. Batching clears the small stuff quickly without wrecking your big tasks.

Here's how to single-task. Before you start, decide the one task and write it on top of a page. Close everything not needed for it, books, tabs, apps. If you remember something else, jot it down and continue. Work until a natural stopping point, like the end of the exercise or the end of a 25-minute timer, before switching.

Here's how to batch. Make a list of small tasks that come up again and again: replying to messages, sharpening pencils and refilling your water bottle, asking parents to sign things, quick tidying. Instead of doing each one when it pops up, do them all in one 15 to 20 minute slot, for example right after school or after dinner. Batch similar things together, like all replies in one go, all errands in one trip to the shop.

Rafi did homework while watching cricket and replying to his friends. Maths took 2 hours and he still got three sums wrong. He changed it: TV off, phone away, one subject at a time. All his chat replies and small chores went into one 20-minute slot after dinner. Maths took 45 minutes with no mistakes, and he still caught the last overs of the match.

The common mistake is thinking you're good at multitasking because you feel busy. Feeling busy is not the same as getting things done. Test it: time yourself doing one homework page with your phone nearby, then without it. The difference usually surprises people.

Remember: big tasks one at a time, small tasks together in a batch.
key_points: Your brain switches between tasks, it doesn't truly do two at once.
Single-tasking: pick one task, close everything else, work to a stopping point.
Batching: group small similar tasks and do them in one 15 to 20 minute slot.
Feeling busy is not the same as getting things done.
lessons.tip: Pick a fixed "small stuff" time each day, like 8:30 pm, and whenever a tiny task pops up earlier, add it to that slot's list instead of doing it right away.
lessons.task: Write down all the small tasks waiting for you right now, like replies, chores and quick favours, and finish them all in one 15-minute batch.

quiz.q: What does your brain actually do when you "multitask"?
options: It switches back and forth very fast, losing time each switch
It does both tasks fully at the same time
It shuts down one side of the brain
It finishes the easier task automatically
quiz.explain: Each switch costs time and attention, which is why multitasking is slower.

quiz.q: Which is an example of batching?
options: Replying to each message the moment it arrives
Studying maths while watching cricket
Replying to all your messages in one 20-minute slot after dinner
Doing one subject at a time with your phone away
quiz.explain: Batching groups small similar tasks into one block of time.

quiz.q: What happened when Rafi single-tasked his maths?
options: It took 2 hours with three mistakes
He missed the whole cricket match
He had to stay up past midnight
It took 45 minutes with no mistakes
quiz.explain: Removing switches made his work faster and more accurate.

lessons.title: Break big projects into milestones
lessons.content:
Imagine climbing a long staircase to the tenth floor. If you stare at the top, it feels impossible. But you never climb ten floors at once. You climb one step, then the next, and you rest at each landing. A milestone is a landing: a clear checkpoint in a big project. Breaking a project into milestones turns one scary mountain into a few small hills.

Without milestones, big projects get left until the end, because "science fair project" is too big to know where to start. Then everything happens in a panic in the last two days. With milestones, you always know the next step, you can see if you're falling behind early, and each finished checkpoint gives you a little boost to keep going.

Here's how. Step one: write the final result clearly. Not "science fair" but "a working water filter model with a poster, ready by 20 March". Step two: list the 3 to 6 big chunks needed to get there, for example: pick the idea, collect materials, build the model, test it, make the poster. Each chunk is a milestone.

Step three: give every milestone a date, working backwards from the deadline. If the fair is on 20 March, maybe the poster is due 18 March, testing 15 March, building done by 12 March, materials by 7 March, idea by 3 March. Step four: break only the first milestone into small tasks you can do this week, like "look at 3 water filter videos" and "ask Abbu for an empty bottle". You'll break the next milestone when you reach it.

Tania had a month to do a solo science project on plants. Last year she had started three days before and cried over a half-done poster. This time she wrote five milestones with dates on a sheet stuck to her wall: choose plant experiment, set up pots, record growth for two weeks, make graph, write poster. She ticked each one off. She finished two days early and won second place in her class.

The common mistake is planning every tiny task for the whole project on day one. Plans change once you start, so detailed lists for week four will be wrong anyway. Plan milestones for the whole project, but small tasks only for the next one.

Remember: define the finish, split it into dated milestones, and plan small steps only for the next one.
key_points: A milestone is a clear checkpoint inside a big project.
Write the final result clearly, then split it into 3 to 6 milestones.
Give each milestone a date, working backwards from the deadline.
Break only the next milestone into small tasks for this week.
lessons.tip: Leave a buffer: set your last milestone at least two days before the real deadline, because something always takes longer than expected.
lessons.task: Pick one big project or exam coming up, write its final result in one sentence, and list 3 to 6 milestones with dates.

quiz.q: What is a milestone?
options: A clear checkpoint inside a big project
The final deadline of a project
A tiny 5-minute task
A reward you get after finishing
quiz.explain: Milestones are the landings on the staircase between start and finish.

quiz.q: How should you set milestone dates?
options: Start from today and guess forwards
Put them all on the deadline day
Don't give milestones dates at all
Work backwards from the deadline
quiz.explain: Working backwards makes sure everything fits before the deadline.

quiz.q: Why plan small tasks only for the next milestone?
options: Small tasks are not useful
Teachers don't allow detailed plans
It's faster to plan nothing at all
Plans change once you start, so far-off details will be wrong anyway
quiz.explain: Plan the big shape for everything, but details only for what's next.

lessons.title: Estimate time honestly
lessons.content:
Ever said "I'll be ready in 5 minutes" and then taken 20? Almost everyone does it. Estimating time means guessing how long a task will really take before you start. Most people guess too short, because they imagine everything going perfectly: no interruptions, no confusion, no searching for a pen.

Bad estimates break your whole day. You plan homework from 4 to 5 and cricket at 5, but homework takes until 6, so you either miss cricket or rush the homework. You start the project "with plenty of time" and end up pulling an all-nighter. Honest estimates let you plan a day that actually works, keep promises to others, and stop feeling always behind.

Here's how to estimate better. Step one: break the task into parts and guess each part, because smaller guesses are more accurate. "Biology homework" becomes "read the section 15 minutes, answer 5 questions 20 minutes, draw the diagram 15 minutes", so 50 minutes. Step two: add a buffer of about half again for surprises. 50 minutes becomes about 75. It feels like too much, but surprises always come.

Step three: learn from reality. Write your guess before you start and the real time after you finish. Do this for a week. You'll notice your personal pattern, for example "I always take about twice as long as I think for writing tasks". Then use that number: if you guess 30 minutes for an essay, plan 60. The more you compare, the better your guesses get.

Sabbir always told his tuition teacher he'd finish practice sheets "in half an hour", and always came to class with them half done. He started writing his guess and the real time in the corner of each sheet. After a week, his guesses were 30 minutes and the real times were about 55. Now he plans an hour for each sheet, starts earlier, and brings complete work every time.

The common mistake is ignoring what happened last time. People think "this time will be faster" again and again. It usually isn't. Trust your record of past times more than your hopeful feeling today.

Remember: break it into parts, add a buffer, and check your guesses against reality.
key_points: Most people guess too short because they imagine no problems.
Break a task into parts and estimate each part.
Add a buffer of about half again for surprises.
Write your guess and the real time to learn your own pattern.
lessons.tip: Write your time guess in the margin before starting any homework, and the real time when you finish. After a week you'll know your personal multiplier.
lessons.task: Pick a task you'll do today, break it into parts, write a time guess for each, add a buffer, then note how long it really took.

quiz.q: Why do most people guess too short?
options: They imagine everything going perfectly with no problems
They are bad at maths
Clocks are usually wrong
Tasks get shorter over time
quiz.explain: Real life has interruptions and confusion that we forget to count.

quiz.q: Your parts add up to 40 minutes. Using the buffer rule, how long should you plan?
options: Exactly 40 minutes
About 20 minutes
About 4 hours
About 60 minutes
quiz.explain: Add about half again for surprises: 40 plus 20 is about 60.

quiz.q: How did Sabbir improve his estimates?
options: He worked faster without checking anything
He told his teacher a shorter time
He wrote his guess and the real time on each sheet for a week
He stopped doing practice sheets
quiz.explain: Comparing guesses to real times showed his pattern, so he planned better.

lessons.title: Time-block your week
lessons.content:
Think of your week like a train timetable. Each train has a fixed slot, so trains don't crash and everyone knows when to be at the station. Time-blocking means giving your important tasks fixed slots on your calendar, like "Monday 5 to 6 pm: chemistry", instead of just hoping you'll find time for them.

A to-do list says what to do, but not when. So tasks float around, and the day fills up with whatever comes first. Without blocks, the important but not urgent work, like revision or practice, keeps getting pushed to tomorrow. With blocks, every important task has a home, you can see if your week is overloaded before it starts, and you stop wasting time deciding what to do next.

Here's how to block a week, ideally during your weekly review. Step one: put in the fixed things first, the ones you can't move: school hours, tuition, coaching, prayer times, family dinner, sleep. Step two: add your top priorities into the empty spaces, using your honest time estimates. For example, "Sunday 4:30 to 5:30, maths chapter 6" and "Tuesday 4:30 to 5:30, English essay".

Step three: add blocks for small stuff batches and for rest and play. Fun goes on the calendar too: cricket, drawing, time with friends. Step four: leave some empty space, roughly an hour on busy days, for things that run late or pop up. Use a paper weekly planner, a table drawn in your copy, or a free calendar app. When a block arrives, do what it says. If something ruins a block, move the task to another slot instead of dropping it.

Nusrat had SSC test exams in three weeks and felt lost. On Saturday she drew a table with days across and hours down. She filled in school, coaching and Maghrib, then put two 50-minute study blocks each weekday, one subject per block, and kept Friday afternoon free for her cousins. When a family wedding ate Tuesday evening, she moved those blocks to Friday morning. She covered every subject before the test.

The common mistake is packing every minute with no breaks or empty space. The first delay knocks over the whole week like dominoes and you give up. A good block plan has gaps on purpose.

Remember: fixed things first, then priorities, then fun, and leave some empty space.
key_points: Time-blocking gives important tasks fixed slots on your calendar.
Fill in fixed things first, then your top priorities.
Put rest and fun on the calendar too.
Leave empty space for delays, and move ruined blocks instead of dropping them.
lessons.tip: Give each block a specific job, like "maths exercise 6.2", not just "study", so you can start the moment the block begins.
lessons.task: Draw a simple table for tomorrow with hours down the side, fill in the fixed things, then add two blocks for your most important tasks and one for fun.

quiz.q: What goes on the weekly plan first?
options: Fun activities like cricket
Small tasks like replying to messages
Fixed things you can't move, like school, tuition and sleep
Whatever you feel like on the day
quiz.explain: Fixed things decide which spaces are left for everything else.

quiz.q: A family wedding takes over Nusrat's Tuesday study blocks. What did she do?
options: Dropped those subjects for the week
Studied during the wedding
Gave up on the whole plan
Moved those blocks to Friday morning
quiz.explain: Move a ruined block to another slot instead of dropping the task.

quiz.q: What is the common mistake with time-blocking?
options: Putting fun on the calendar
Packing every minute with no empty space
Planning during the weekly review
Giving each block a specific job
quiz.explain: Without gaps, one delay knocks the whole week over.

lessons.title: Get group work done
lessons.content:
Group work is like a cricket team. If all eleven players run for the same ball, the other side scores easily. Each player needs a position: bowler, keeper, slip, deep fine leg. A group project works the same way. It goes well when everyone knows their job, the deadline for it, and how the team will talk.

Without a plan, group work goes wrong in familiar ways. One person does everything and feels angry. Two people do the same part and nobody does another. The group chat fills with "so what are we doing?" until the night before submission. With a simple plan, the work gets shared fairly, nothing gets missed, and you actually finish early.

Here's how to set it up in the first meeting, which can be 15 minutes at tiffin break. Step one: agree on the final result together. What exactly are you submitting, how long, and by when? Step two: split the work into clear parts and give each part one owner by name. For example: "Rafi, research and 3 facts by Tuesday. Tania, poster design by Thursday. Sabbir, the speech by Thursday. Nusrat, putting it all together on Saturday."

Step three: write the plan down where everyone can see it, like a pinned message in the group chat, with names and dates. Step four: agree on short check-ins, for example a 5-minute talk every second day at school, or one message each evening: "done, doing, stuck". If someone is stuck, help early instead of waiting. If someone isn't doing their part, talk to them kindly first, and if that fails, tell your teacher early, not on the last day.

Last year Sabbir's group of four had a social science project. Nobody planned, so he ended up doing almost all of it at 1 am. This year he suggested a 15-minute tiffin meeting. They split the work into four parts, each with a name and a date, and pinned it in the group chat. Every evening each person sent one line. They finished a day early, and for once nobody was angry.

The common mistake is splitting work as "everyone does a bit of everything" or leaving owners vague, like "we'll all do research". When a job belongs to everybody, it belongs to nobody. Every part needs exactly one name.

Remember: agree on the goal, give every part one owner and a date, write it down, and check in often.
key_points: Agree together on what you're submitting and by when.
Split the work into parts and give each part one named owner and a date.
Write the plan where everyone can see it, like a pinned group chat message.
Do short check-ins, and raise problems early, not on the last day.
lessons.tip: End every group meeting by having each person say out loud what they'll do and by when, then pin those lines in the group chat.
lessons.task: Think of a current or recent group task and write a plan for it: the final result, 3 to 5 parts, one name and one date for each part.

quiz.q: In a group plan, how many owners should each part have?
options: Everyone in the group
Nobody, people choose on the day
Exactly one named person
Two people who share it equally
quiz.explain: When a job belongs to everybody, it belongs to nobody.

quiz.q: What did Sabbir's group do differently this year?
options: Let Sabbir do all the work again
Held a short tiffin meeting and pinned a plan with names and dates
Started the night before submission
Worked without talking to each other
quiz.explain: A short meeting and a visible plan shared the work fairly.

quiz.q: A teammate isn't doing their part. What does the lesson suggest?
options: Talk to them kindly first, then tell the teacher early if needed
Quietly do their part yourself at night
Tell the teacher on the last day
Remove them from the group chat
quiz.explain: Raise the problem early, kindly first, while there is still time to fix it.

lessons.title: Match tasks to your peak hours
lessons.content:
Your energy is like the tide at Cox's Bazar. It goes up and down through the day in a pattern. Most people have a time when their brain is sharpest, often a few hours after waking, and a slump, often after lunch. Matching tasks to your peak hours means doing your hardest thinking when your energy is high, and saving easy jobs for when it's low.

If you get this backwards, you waste your best hours. Many students spend their fresh morning on easy things like scrolling or chatting, then try to learn tough maths at 11 pm when their brain is half asleep. It takes twice as long and still doesn't stick. When you put hard work in your peak time, the same task feels easier and goes faster.

Here's how to find your peak. For 3 to 5 days, rate your energy from 1 to 5 every two hours or so, and jot it in a note: "8 am: 3, 10 am: 5, 2 pm: 2, 5 pm: 4, 9 pm: 2". Pay attention to when focusing feels easy and when your eyes start drooping. Look for your highest and lowest numbers. Many people find a high in the morning and another, smaller high in the late afternoon.

Then sort your tasks into three types. Hard thinking tasks, like new maths, physics problems or writing an essay, go in your peak hours. Medium tasks, like revision or reading, go in the medium hours. Easy tasks, like packing your bag, copying notes, tidying or replying to messages, go in the slump. On school days, your peak may be in class, so use your best free slot, for example straight after an afternoon snack. Also protect your sleep, because a tired brain has no real peak.

Rafi always did his hardest homework at 10 pm after watching TV, and kept making silly mistakes. He tracked his energy for four days and found his afternoon high was at 4:30 to 6 pm, after a snack and a short rest. He moved maths to 4:30 and left easy stuff like copying notes for after dinner. His mistakes dropped and he went to bed an hour earlier.

The common mistake is copying someone else's schedule, like "successful people wake at 5 am". Your peak is yours. Some people are sharp early, others later. Track your own energy and plan around it, while still getting enough sleep.

Remember: find your sharpest hours, and put your hardest task there.
key_points: Your energy goes up and down through the day in a pattern.
Track your energy from 1 to 5 for a few days to find your peak and slump.
Do hard thinking tasks in your peak and easy tasks in your slump.
Your peak is personal, so don't just copy someone else's routine.
lessons.tip: Save a list of easy "slump tasks", like sharpening pencils or sorting notes, so when your energy drops you still get something useful done.
lessons.task: Start an energy log today: write your energy from 1 to 5 right now and set a reminder to rate it again every two hours until bedtime.

quiz.q: Which task belongs in your peak energy hours?
options: Packing your school bag
Replying to messages
Tidying your desk
Learning a new maths chapter
quiz.explain: Hard thinking tasks need your sharpest brain.

quiz.q: How do you find your peak hours?
options: Ask a friend when they study best
Rate your energy from 1 to 5 every couple of hours for a few days
Always study at 5 am like successful people
Study only when you feel like it
quiz.explain: Your own record shows your real pattern.

quiz.q: What did Rafi change after tracking his energy?
options: He started studying at midnight
He stopped doing homework on weekdays
He drank more tea at 10 pm
He moved maths to 4:30 pm and easy tasks to after dinner
quiz.explain: Putting hard work in his afternoon high cut his mistakes.

lessons.title: The 80/20 rule and good enough
lessons.content:
Imagine you're cleaning your room before guests arrive in 15 minutes. Clearing the bed and the floor makes the room look mostly clean. Polishing every shelf would take an hour and barely anyone would notice. That's the 80/20 rule: often, a small part of the effort, roughly 20 percent, gives most of the result, roughly 80 percent. The numbers are not exact. The idea is that some work matters much more than the rest.

Without this idea, you spend hours on the parts that don't matter much, like decorating a title for 40 minutes, and run out of time for the part that gets the marks. Or you keep polishing one thing forever because it isn't perfect. With 80/20 thinking, you put your effort where it pays off, finish on time, and stop wearing yourself out chasing perfect.

Here's how to use it. Before a task, ask: which few parts give most of the result? For an exam, that's usually the topics that come up most often and carry the most marks. Check past papers and your syllabus to find them. For a project, it's the parts the teacher grades, not the fancy borders. Do those parts first and do them well.

Then decide what "good enough" looks like before you start. Write it down: "Poster has a clear title, 3 key facts, 1 diagram, no spelling mistakes." When you reach that, you're done, or you add extras only if you have spare time. Good enough doesn't mean sloppy. It means meeting the real standard without wasting hours on tiny improvements nobody asked for.

Nusrat used to spend most of her revision time making beautiful colourful notes for every chapter, and ran out of time to practise questions. Before her final exam, she looked at the last five years' papers and noticed that four chapters carried most of the marks. She practised questions from those first, kept her notes simple, and covered the rest lightly. Her marks went up, and she slept properly the night before.

The common mistake is using 80/20 as an excuse to skip things completely. The other 20 percent of results still matters, especially in exams where any chapter can appear. The rule tells you what to do first and best, not what to ignore forever.

Remember: find the few parts that matter most, do them first, and stop at good enough.
key_points: A small part of the work often gives most of the result.
Find the high-value parts first, like exam topics that carry the most marks.
Decide what "good enough" looks like before you start.
80/20 decides what to do first, not what to skip forever.
lessons.tip: Before you start any project, write one line: "Done means..." and list 3 to 4 things it needs. Stop polishing when they're all there.
lessons.task: Take one subject's syllabus or past paper and circle the 3 topics that carry the most marks, then plan to revise those first this week.

quiz.q: What does the 80/20 rule say?
options: You should work 80 hours and rest 20
Always finish 80 percent of tasks and skip 20 percent
A small part of the effort often gives most of the result
Work 20 minutes and rest 80 minutes
quiz.explain: The numbers are rough, but some work matters much more than the rest.

quiz.q: How did Nusrat find which chapters mattered most?
options: She picked the shortest chapters
She asked which chapters were easiest
She looked at the last five years' exam papers
She made colourful notes for every chapter
quiz.explain: Past papers showed which chapters carried most of the marks.

quiz.q: What is the common mistake with the 80/20 rule?
options: Using it as an excuse to skip the rest completely
Doing the high-value parts first
Deciding what good enough means
Checking past papers
quiz.explain: The rule sets your order, but the rest still matters, especially in exams.

lessons.title: Get back on track after a bad week
lessons.content:
Imagine you're riding a bicycle and you wobble off the path into the grass. You don't throw the bicycle away. You stop, steer back onto the path and keep riding. A bad week is that wobble. Maybe you were sick, there was a wedding, or you just lost motivation and your routine fell apart. Getting back on track means restarting quickly and calmly, without trying to fix everything at once.

The real damage of a bad week isn't the week itself. It's what comes after: "I've already ruined it, so what's the point?" One missed week turns into a missed month. Or you panic and try to catch up on everything in one night, burn out and fall behind again. If you know how to restart, a bad week is just a small bump.

Here's a simple restart plan. Step one: don't punish yourself. Say, "That week went badly. That's normal. I'm restarting today." Step two: do a quick reset, 15 minutes. Write every pending task on one list, check what's actually due soon, and delete or postpone anything that no longer matters. Usually the list is shorter than it felt.

Step three: pick just the top 3 things that are most urgent and important, like the assignment due Monday and the test on Wednesday. Ignore the rest for now. Step four: restart your habits at a smaller size. If you used to study 2 hours, start with 30 minutes today. If you did 20 push-ups, do 5. Getting back into motion matters more than the amount. Over the next few days, grow it back to normal.

Sabbir got dengue and missed nine days of school. When he recovered, he looked at his pile of missed work and felt like giving up. His mother helped him make one list. He asked a friend for class notes, checked dates, and found only three things due soon. He did those first, studying 40 minutes a day at the start, then back to his normal 90 minutes by the second week. Within three weeks he had caught up.

The common mistake is waiting for a "fresh start" like next Monday or the first of the month. Waiting adds more days to the bad stretch. The best day to restart is today, with a small step.

Remember: no guilt, one list, top 3 tasks, and restart small today.
key_points: A bad week is normal, and the danger is giving up afterwards.
Do a 15-minute reset: one list, check due dates, delete what no longer matters.
Pick only the top 3 urgent and important tasks to start.
Restart habits at a smaller size, today, not next Monday.
lessons.tip: Keep a "minimum day" plan for hard times, like 20 minutes of study and 5 push-ups. On bad days, doing just the minimum keeps the chain alive.
lessons.task: Write your own minimum day plan: the smallest version of your study and other habits that you could do even on your worst day.

quiz.q: According to the lesson, what is the real danger of a bad week?
options: Thinking "it's ruined anyway" and giving up afterwards
Losing all your friends
Being punished at school
Forgetting how to study forever
quiz.explain: The week is a bump. Giving up after it is what turns it into a long fall.

quiz.q: After nine sick days, what did Sabbir do first?
options: Tried to finish all missed work in one night
Waited for the first of the next month
Skipped all the missed work
Made one list, checked dates, and did the three tasks due soon
quiz.explain: One list and the top few tasks made the pile manageable.

quiz.q: When is the best time to restart after a bad week?
options: Next Monday
Today, with a small step
The first day of next month
When you feel fully motivated
quiz.explain: Waiting for a fresh start just adds more lost days.

lessons.title: Build your own productivity system
lessons.content:
Think of the tools from this course like the parts of a bicycle: wheels, chain, brakes, handlebar. Each part is useful, but you only go somewhere when they're put together. A personal productivity system is your own simple set of habits and tools that work together: where you catch tasks, how you choose what matters, when you plan, and how you protect your focus.

Without a system, you use a trick for a few days, then forget it and go back to chaos. You keep starting over. With a simple system, these tools run every day and every week without much thinking, so you stay on top of school, home and your own goals, even in busy or stressful weeks.

Here's a simple system you can build from what you've learned. Daily: catch everything in one inbox as it comes up. Each evening, take 10 minutes to clear the inbox and write tomorrow's list of 3 to 5 tasks with one starred task. During the day, do your starred task in your peak hours, use pomodoros for focus, keep your phone out of sight, and batch small tasks into one slot.

Weekly: once a week, do your 15 to 20 minute review. Look back, clear up, check next week's calendar, pick your top 3 goals, and time-block the main study sessions, fun and empty space. For big projects, set milestones with dates and break only the next one into tasks. Keep your tools few: one notebook or one notes app, one calendar, one inbox. More tools means more places for things to get lost.

Tania tried a new app every month and never stuck with any. She decided to keep it simple: one small notebook with an inbox page at the back, a daily list at the front, and a weekly review every Friday after Jumma using a paper calendar. At first she forgot the evening routine twice a week, so she linked it to after-dinner tea. Three months later, she rarely missed deadlines and felt calmer before exams.

The common mistake is building a giant, perfect system on day one, with colour codes, five apps and a two-hour weekly plan. It collapses within a week. Start with just two pieces, an inbox and a daily list, use them for two weeks, then add the weekly review, then time-blocking. A small system you use beats a perfect one you don't.

Remember: one inbox, a daily list, a weekly review, and add more only when those stick.
key_points: A productivity system is a simple set of habits and tools that work together.
Daily: one inbox, a 10-minute evening plan, the starred task in your peak hours.
Weekly: a 15 to 20 minute review, top 3 goals and time blocks.
Start with two pieces and add more only when they stick.
lessons.tip: Keep everything in as few tools as possible: one notebook or notes app, one calendar. If you find yourself checking four places, merge them.
lessons.task: Write your system on one page: where your inbox is, when you'll do your 10-minute evening plan, and which day and time you'll do your weekly review.

quiz.q: What should you start with when building your system?
options: Five apps with colour codes
Just two pieces, an inbox and a daily list
A two-hour weekly plan
Every tool from the course on day one
quiz.explain: A small system you actually use beats a perfect one that collapses.

quiz.q: How did Tania stop forgetting her evening routine?
options: She downloaded a new app
She linked it to her after-dinner tea
She did it only on weekends
She gave up the evening routine
quiz.explain: Linking it to an existing habit, like in the habits lesson, made it stick.

quiz.q: Why does the lesson say to keep your tools few?
options: More tools means more places for things to get lost
Tools are expensive
Teachers check your tools
Fewer tools look neater
quiz.explain: One notebook, one calendar and one inbox keep everything in sight.
